column4: This is the exact Qur'anic reprise of the image: feared عَيْلَة is answered by God's future يُغْنِيكُم from His bounty.
The poor are brought into a household through marriage and God promises يُغْنِهِمُ ٱللَّهُ مِن فَضْلِهِ, matching sufficiency placed in another's hand.
أَغْنَىٰ وَأَقْنَىٰ names God as both the giver of wealth and the giver of enduring possessions, exactly the section's two definitions of riches.
أَنتُمُ ٱلْفُقَرَآءُ إِلَى ٱللَّهِ and God's being ٱلْغَنِىُّ make creaturely need and true independence face one another.
In a call to spend, stinginess harms the miser himself because وَٱللَّهُ ٱلْغَنِىُّ وَأَنتُمُ ٱلْفُقَرَآءُ; this joins poverty, divine sufficiency, and acquisitive withholding.
After watering the women's flock, Moses says he is فَقِيرٌ for any خَيْر God sends; need, beneficial provision, and the provider are all explicit.
The restrained poor are mistaken for أَغْنِيَآءَ and do not ask insistently, sharpening the section's identification of a poor person with a sā'il by showing the silent case.
The allocation includes orphans, the needy, and the traveler so property will not circulate only بَيْنَ ٱلْأَغْنِيَآءِ, giving the social consequence of wealth placed in one's hand.
Those who do not يَجِدُونَ means for marriage must remain chaste until God يُغْنِيَهُم; it joins the section's “finding” and “enriching” senses beside 24:32.
If spouses separate, يُغْنِ ٱللَّهُ كُلًّا مِّن سَعَتِهِ promises that God can make each sufficient from His abundance.
Satan promises poverty and urges indecency, while God promises forgiveness and bounty; it exposes fear of want as the seed of grasping.
Provision comes from where the servant does not reckon, God is enough for the one who trusts Him, and He has set a measure for everything.
The affluent and the constrained each spend from what God has given, and سَيَجْعَلُ ٱللَّهُ بَعْدَ عُسْرٍ يُسْرًا states the movement from straitness to ease.
إِن تَرَكَ خَيْرًا uses khayr for property left at death, the precise secondary sense of خَيْر developed in the section.
A kind word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by hurt, and God's being غَنِىٌّ frames how the former needy person should receive a petitioner.
The command to spend from the good things one has earned and not select the bad makes concrete the section's “abundant and cleanly acquired” sense of wealth; God is غَنِىٌّ.
Their wealth contains a recognized right لِّلسَّآئِلِ وَٱلْمَحْرُومِ, placing the asker and the deprived at the possessor's door.
The worshippers' wealth contains a known right, so possession is presented as carrying an obligation rather than conferring independence; 70:25 names its recipients.
لِّلسَّآئِلِ وَٱلْمَحْرُومِ names both the asking poor person and the one deprived without asking, completing 70:24's rule for wealth.
The distributed property is specifically for poor emigrants expelled from homes and possessions, a concrete state of need beside 59:7's limit on rich-only circulation.
The hosts prefer the migrants over themselves وَلَوْ كَانَ بِهِمْ خَصَاصَةٌ, turning one's own scarcity away from the acquisitive greed the section names.
The rich guardian must abstain while the poor guardian may consume reasonably, making wealth and poverty determine a measured use of another's property.
True goodness includes giving beloved wealth to relatives, orphans, the needy, travelers, and ٱلسَّآئِلِينَ, the section's poor-as-asker made an object of care.
Obligatory alms are assigned first to ٱلْفُقَرَآءِ and the needy, showing wealth deliberately moved into the hands of those lacking it.
The relative, needy person, and traveler are each to receive their due, directly staging the encounter between a possessor and someone in need.
If one must turn the needy away while awaiting provision from the Lord, one must still speak gently; this specifies how not to rebuff the petitioner of 17:26.
Asked what to spend, the verse calls the spendable property خَيْر and directs it to parents, kin, orphans, the needy, and travelers.
A town once secure with abundant provision denies God's favors and is made to taste hunger and fear, reversing niʿmah's pleasant livelihood into bodily want.
The Lord of the House أَطْعَمَهُم مِّن جُوعٍ, a compact image of a provider removing the bodily mark of poverty.
The food of punishment neither nourishes nor يُغْنِى مِن جُوعٍ; the sufficiency sense of the source's agnā branch is denied at the exact point of hunger.
When his Lord honors him and gives him نعمة, the human calls himself honored; the verse directly tests the section's link between niʿmah and comfortable living.
When his provision is measured tightly, the human says his Lord has humiliated him; it marks the boundary between material straitness and true worth.
كَلَّا rejects that inference and identifies the real failure as not honoring the orphan, reversing the conduct commanded around the poverty image.
Failure to urge feeding the poor makes neglect of bodily need, rather than restricted provision itself, part of the preceding moral diagnosis.
Consuming inheritance wholesale turns acquired property into predation, the corrupt counterpart to wealth received and shared as provision.
Loving wealth with consuming love gives a Qur'anic form to the acquisitive craving that the section calls poverty's trace in the soul.
Feeding on a day of مَسْغَبَة confronts hunger as the bodily form of poverty; 90:15–16 identify who is fed.
An orphan of near kin is the first person named in the feeding scene, linking material sufficiency to the surah's neighboring care for the orphan.
مِسْكِينًا ذَا مَتْرَبَةٍ depicts the needy person reduced to dust, the concrete recipient of the food in 90:14.
The denier يَدُعُّ ٱلْيَتِيمَ, a direct reversal of the surrounding surah's commands not to overpower or rebuff the vulnerable visitor.
Not urging the food of the poor turns the bodily need behind the image into the test the denier fails.
They give food, despite loving or needing it, to a needy person, orphan, and captive, answering hunger without treating possession as self-sufficiency.
Joseph's brothers arrive afflicted with hardship and scant goods, ask for full measure and charity, and thus stage needy petition before one able to supply.
The poor donors who لَا يَجِدُونَ إِلَّا جُهْدَهُمْ give the little they can find, joining the “find/means” sense with generosity under constraint.
There is no blame on those who لَا يَجِدُونَ مَا يُنفِقُونَ, a direct case in which not “finding” means lacking property to spend.
Those denied mounts because the Prophet can find none leave weeping that they lack anything to spend, embodying unmet material need without acquisitive pride.
Housing is required مِن وُجْدِكُم, according to one's means, a Qur'anic use of the “finding” root for material capacity close to the source dictionary sense.
At Midian's water Moses finds two women holding back their animals because their father is old; this is the needy scene his act in 28:24 answers.
One woman returns with an invitation to reward Moses for watering, showing provision arriving immediately after the confession of poverty in 28:24.
The proposal to hire Moses turns his strength and trustworthiness into livelihood, one concrete way the prayer of 28:24 is answered.
Work and marriage are joined in the father's offer, so the needy stranger is given both livelihood and household after 28:24.
God reminds a once weak and fearful community that He sheltered, supported, and provided them good things, a collective movement from vulnerability to sufficiency.
Unlimited provision would make people transgress, so God sends it down in a measured amount; sufficiency is distinguished from acquisitive excess.
God apportions livelihoods and ranks in worldly life, while the Lord's mercy is better than what people accumulate; need, measure, and acquisitions meet in one verse.
The Prophet must not covet others' temporary splendor because وَرِزْقُ رَبِّكَ خَيْرٌ وَأَبْقَىٰ, joining better provision to what remains.
What people possess runs out while what is with God remains, setting accumulated holdings against lasting sufficiency.
God expands and measures provision as He wills, denying that material abundance is self-produced or an unqualified mark of favor.
Wealth and children do not bring anyone near to God; possession is bounded as neither spiritual sufficiency nor self-bestowed rank.
God expands or measures provision and promises to replace whatever is spent, answering the fear that giving will create poverty.
God expands and measures provision, and worldly life is only a brief enjoyment beside the Hereafter, joining material measure to 93:4's scale of better things.
The Lord expands and measures provision for whom He wills, locating both plenty and straitness in the provider's knowledge.
Hunger and loss of wealth are named as trials, making explicit both the bodily and material faces of the section's darlık.
Many creatures cannot carry their own provision; God provides for them and for people, making dependence on the giver visible.
The challenge asks who could provide if God withheld His provision, defining dependence by imagining the provider's gift removed.
God يُطْعِمُ وَلَا يُطْعَمُ: He feeds and is not fed, the provider's independence set against every creature's need.
God gives from all that people ask and His نعمة cannot be counted, yet the human is deeply ungrateful; asking, gift, and acknowledgment meet.
The earth's sustenances are measured سَوَآءً لِّلسَّآئِلِينَ; if “those who ask” here includes creatures seeking provision, it widens the poor-as-sā'il image to universal dependence.
Hidden charity given to the poor is called better for the donors, joining material aid, khayr, and restraint from exposing the recipient.
Every نعمة is from God, and distress makes people cry to Him; comfortable living is explicitly traced back to its giver.
Gratitude for blessing is answered with increase, so acknowledged provision grows rather than becoming a title of self-sufficiency.
The people of Sheba are told to eat their Lord's provision and thank Him, presenting good livelihood as a gift to be acknowledged.
When they turn away, the two fruitful gardens are replaced by bitter, sparse produce; comfortable provision reverses into insufficiency.
The one who gives and remains mindful stands opposite the grasping “self-sufficient” person introduced in 92:8.
God promises to ease the giver toward ease, a neighboring promise that makes 92:8's self-sufficiency part of a moral fork.
The miser بَخِلَ وَٱسْتَغْنَىٰ claims independence through withholding, the precise reversal of being made sufficient by another in 93:8.
The miser is eased toward hardship, reversing the movement from poverty to sufficiency and completing the consequence of 92:8.
وَمَا يُغْنِى عَنْهُ مَالُهُۥ denies that his wealth will suffice when he falls, exposing false self-sufficiency in the very agnā sense the section develops.
Human transgression is the consequence stated immediately before the person's seeing himself as self-sufficient in 96:7.
أَن رَّءَاهُ ٱسْتَغْنَىٰ makes self-perceived independence, rather than received sufficiency, the cause of rebellion.
Frowning begins a scene of receiving a vulnerable visitor badly, the enacted opposite of not rebuking the petitioner.
The reason for the frown is that the blind man came to him; this identifies the visitor whose reception 80:1 judges.
The person who ٱسْتَغْنَىٰ receives attention, making presumed self-sufficiency the social status preferred over the vulnerable visitor.
Giving oneself eagerly to the self-sufficient person completes the misplaced preference introduced in 80:5.
The other person comes striving, an active seeker whose approach helps specify the vulnerable visitor of the rebuke scene.
Being distracted from the earnest visitor completes the reversal of the command not to drive away the one who comes asking.
The human is described as anxiously grasping, introducing the inward disposition that appears as panic in want and withholding in plenty.
When harm touches him he becomes frantic, the scarcity-side of the acquisitive disposition completed in 70:21.
When good touches him he withholds, turning received plenty into the soul-level greed the section identifies as poverty's trace.
The human's fierce حُبِّ ٱلْخَيْرِ uses khayr for wealth and exposes attachment to acquisition rather than measured sufficiency.
Even owners of God's treasuries would withhold for fear of spending; imagined abundance fails to cure the fear of lack.
Those stingy with what God gave from His bounty think it good for them, but the withheld property becomes a collar, denying that possession itself is khayr.
A person promises charity and righteousness if God gives from His bounty, staging poverty's hoped-for transition before 9:76 tests it.
Once God gives from His bounty, they become stingy and turn away, showing received sufficiency converted into acquisitive withholding.
Wealth advanced to increase through others' property does not grow with God, while alms given for God are multiplied; it separates grasping increase from fruitful giving.
Those who are stingy and command stinginess are answered by God's being ٱلْغَنِىُّ ٱلْحَمِيدُ, true independence confronting hoarded wealth.
مَآ أَغْنَىٰ عَنِّى مَالِيَهْ is the ruined person's admission that property did not suffice, a direct boundary on monetary ghina.
مَآ أَغْنَىٰ عَنْهُ مَالُهُۥ وَمَا كَسَبَ denies sufficiency to both held wealth and acquisition.
The disbelievers' wealth and children will not تُغْنِىَ عَنْهُم before God, so worldly abundance cannot meet the decisive need.
Again wealth and children cannot suffice before God, reinforcing the limit on possessions as a source of independence.
The أصحاب الأعراف ask the proud rich what their gathering and arrogance أَغْنَىٰ for them, exposing accumulated company or property as failed sufficiency.
At Hunayn the believers' great numbers do not تُغْنِ عنهم شيئًا, extending the boundary of sufficiency from possessions to human abundance.
Long enjoyment does not أَغْنَىٰ when punishment arrives, marking temporal plenty as unable to secure lasting welfare.
What earlier peoples earned did not أَغْنَىٰ for them, opposing acquired gain to the sufficiency only the giver can secure.
The former nations' greater power and earnings do not أَغْنَىٰ for them, another direct limit on acquisitions as sufficiency.
Neither their earnings nor adopted protectors يُغْنِى عَنْهُم, showing that possessions and dependencies alike can fail the need they promise to meet.
Wealth and children will never تُغْنِىَ عَنْهُم before God, denying the richest household ultimate independence.
What the people of the Stone had earned did not أَغْنَىٰ for them, a concise reversal of acquisition imagined as security.
The garden owner boasts that he has more wealth and a stronger following, treating comparative possession as a self-made rank.
His companion tells him to acknowledge God's will and power even if the companion has less wealth and children, relocating sufficiency in the giver.
The garden's produce is destroyed and its owner wrings his hands over what he spent, making accumulated wealth visibly pass away.
Wealth and children are worldly adornment, while lasting good deeds are خَيْر with the Lord in reward and hope; it pairs 93:4's “better” with possessions that pass.
Qarun's immense treasuries and exultation stage wealth as acquisitive excess rather than enoughness received with humility.
Qarun is told to seek the Hereafter with what God gave him and to do good as God did good to him, turning received property into transmitted benefit.
Qarun claims the wealth was given because of knowledge he possesses, the narrative form of taking conferred richness as a self-bestowed title.
Those desiring worldly life envy Qarun's mighty fortune, showing how visible acquisitions awaken the soul's craving.
The knowledgeable answer that God's reward is better, restoring the “better latter” scale against Qarun's displayed wealth.
Qarun and his house are swallowed, and no party can help him, so possessions and status fail as sufficiency.
The former admirers recognize that God expands and measures provision and that worldly success does not prove divine favor.
The owners of a garden are tested when they resolve to harvest in the morning, beginning a scene in which possession meets the poor person's claim.
Their plan is that no needy person enter the garden, a direct reversal of welcoming the poor person who arrives at one's provision.
They go out determined to withhold, showing acquisitive resolve immediately before their imagined sufficiency collapses.
On seeing the ruined garden they say they are مَحْرُومُونَ, becoming the deprived people they had meant to exclude.
They hope their Lord will replace the garden with something better, returning failed possession to dependence on the giver.
God identifies the wealthy opponent as one He created alone, placing his later abundance against his original utter dependence.
God says He placed extensive wealth in the man's hand, explicitly identifying another as the source of his possessions.
God says He made life smooth for him, matching the section's definition of niʿmah as ease and pleasant living.
After extensive wealth and ease, the man still covets increase, a precise instance of plenty failing to end acquisitive need.
The question asks whether wealth and sons are mistaken for God's hastening خَيْرَات to their owners, challenging property read as assured good.
كَل لَّا يَشْعُرُونَ rejects that inference, bounding visible plenty as neither moral good nor proof of favor.
The claim إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ فَقِيرٌ وَنَحْنُ أَغْنِيَآءُ blasphemously reverses the creaturely poverty and divine richness stated in 35:15.
Justice must not bend for either rich or poor because God is closer to both, preventing material status from controlling moral judgment.
Pilgrimage binds duty to human ability, then declares God غَنِىٌّ عَنِ ٱلْعَٰلَمِينَ; creaturely capacity is measured while God needs none of it.
Even universal ingratitude leaves God غَنِىٌّ حَمِيدٌ, so acknowledged blessing benefits the receiver rather than supplying a need in the giver.
Gratitude benefits oneself, while disbelief cannot diminish the Lord who is غَنِىٌّ كَرِيمٌ; true richness is joined to generosity.
Wisdom directs gratitude because it benefits the grateful person, whereas God remains غَنِىٌّ حَمِيدٌ, separating received blessing from the giver's need.
Because everything in heaven and earth belongs to God, He is ٱلْغَنِىُّ ٱلْحَمِيدُ; possession and independence coincide only for the universal owner.
Whatever people are given is temporary worldly enjoyment, while what is with God is خَيْرٌ وَأَبْقَىٰ, the same scale that places lasting good above present property.
Worldly gifts are temporary enjoyment, but what is with God is خَيْرٌ وَأَبْقَىٰ, distinguishing holdings from lasting sufficiency.
People prefer the nearer life, identifying the preference that 87:17 and 93:4 correct.
وَٱلْءَاخِرَةُ خَيْرٌ وَأَبْقَىٰ directly matches the surah's claim that the latter is better while adding that it remains.
Worldly life becomes rivalry in multiplying wealth and children before its growth withers, making acquisitions visibly abundant and passing.
Competition for increase distracts people, reducing the “many acquisitions” definition of wealth to a hunger that never becomes enough.
The slanderer gathers wealth and repeatedly counts it, a compact portrait of acquisitive craving.
He thinks his wealth makes him last, mistaking possession for lasting sufficiency.
Contentment with nearer life over the Hereafter is rebuked because worldly enjoyment is little, reinforcing the image's better-latter scale.
The promise that one will neither hunger nor be unclothed marks a boundary state in which the bodily signs of poverty are absent.
Those told to spend God's provision refuse by asking whether they should feed someone God could feed, exposing a false appeal to the provider used to rebuff the needy.
A debtor in hardship must receive respite until ease, and remission is better, turning financial straitness into a claim on the creditor's mercy.
Feeding ten needy people from the average food of one's household gives material “enoughness” a measured legal form.
Every creature's provision rests with God, universalizing the section's relation between the needy being and the one who places sustenance in its reach.
God desires no provision from creatures and does not ask them to feed Him, denying every mark of need in the giver.
God is ٱلرَّزَّاقُ, possessor of power, completing 51:57's contrast between the provider and those who must be provided for.
The condemned person did not urge feeding the poor, making neglect of hunger a failure with lasting consequence.
The condemned confess that they did not feed the needy, another direct reversal of letting received provision answer another's want.
